summary:
This run covered 18 evals (34 iterations), with trigger detection firing 100% of the time across all applicable evals. Two evals ("throttling-question-does-not-trigger" and "neg-invoke-access-denied") were intentionally skipped (should_trigger: false), so they contribute no data either way.

**Expected-output and assertion pass rates:** Across most of the 16 scored evals, with_skill met the overall "expected output" bar more often than without_skill. In roughly 11 of the 16 scored evals, with_skill passed expected_output (1/1) while without_skill failed (0/1); in several of these (e.g. scp-impact-before-applying, no-guardrail-on-production-path, pii-entry-with-only-action, invocation-log-input-assessment-is-not-detection, version-limit-counts-draft) with_skill also swept or nearly swept the per-assertion checks (often 100%) while without_skill passed a meaningfully smaller fraction (14%-71%). A few evals (tool-results-not-evaluated, grounding-score-near-threshold-invented-fact, guardrail-latency-streaming) show both variants passing expected_output and similar or identical assertion pass rates, indicating these behaviors are already well-handled by both. One eval (draft-not-pinned-trap) could not compare assertions for without_skill because that variant's run was inconclusive/produced no scorable output (0s runtime, $0 cost), so no assertion data exists for it there.

Two evals are weaker measurement cases: "full-report-connected-accounts" and "guardduty-anomalous-invocation" show expected_output failing for BOTH variants (0/1 each), with several assertions in "always_fails" pattern for both — meaning these specific behaviors/assertions are not being satisfied by either variant and likely point to a gap in the underlying behavior or the assertion itself rather than a difference between variants. Within these, with_skill still cleared more individual assertions than without_skill in one case and fewer in the other (mixed), so no consistent direction emerges there.

**Per-assertion patterns:** Several assertions show "always_fails" for both variants (e.g., docs.aws.amazon.com citation checks in a few evals, re-enabling/inactive-key distinctions, resolving which guardrail is referenced) — these indicate the behavior itself is not yet reliably produced by either variant and the assertion is not discriminating between them. Other assertions show "always_passes" for both (e.g., not exposing account IDs, not claiming to have modified resources, avoiding full key exposure) — these are consistently satisfied and also not differentiating. The assertions that do differentiate skew toward a "with_skill passes / without_skill fails" pattern much more often than the reverse; the reverse pattern ("without_skill passes / with_skill fails") appears rarely (e.g., one assertion each in guardduty-anomalous-invocation and inactive-admin-key).

**Runtime and cost:** Results are mixed and do not track consistently with quality outcomes. In several evals without_skill ran faster and cheaper (e.g., inactive-admin-key: 29s/$0.25 vs with_skill's 1m52s/$0.93; invocation-log-input-assessment-is-not-detection: 10s/$0.09 vs 23s/$0.19), while in scp-impact-before-applying without_skill ran much longer and cost more (5m47s/$2.89 vs with_skill's 1m42s/$0.85). In a couple of cases (draft-not-pinned-trap, grounding-score-far-below-threshold) without_skill shows 0s/$0.00, suggesting no meaningful run was recorded for that variant on that eval, which limits comparability there. Where both variants did run, without_skill was often somewhat faster/cheaper, but this coincides with lower assertion and expected-output pass rates in many of those same evals — a speed/cost vs. thoroughness tradeoff rather than a strict advantage.

**Quality comparison (head-to-head judged pairs):** Direct quality comparisons were only computed for 4 of the 18 evals (tool-results-not-evaluated, guardrail-latency-streaming, grounding-score-near-threshold-invented-fact), with the rest skipped (pairs_skipped: 1) — meaning quality-comparison data is sparse and should be read as a thin signal. In two of these three, without_skill was favored on accuracy/actionability/completeness criteria (tool-results-not-evaluated, guardrail-latency-streaming), while grounding-score-near-threshold-invented-fact was split, with each variant favored on one criterion and one comparable. These judgments carry only "medium" average confidence, so they're directionally suggestive rather than conclusive, and notably run counter to the broader expected-output/assertion pattern favoring with_skill in those same evals' other assertions.

**Output consistency:** No output-consistency data was reported (all null) for any eval, so repeat-run stability could not be assessed for either variant in this dataset.

**Overall picture:** Across most evals with usable data, with_skill more often met the defined expected output and passed a higher share of assertions, sometimes by a wide margin, while without_skill was frequently faster and cheaper to run. Two evals show both variants failing the expected-output bar on the same assertions, pointing to areas where neither variant handles the behavior well yet. The handful of directly judged quality comparisons that exist are sparse, carry only medium confidence, and in a couple of cases favor without_skill's output quality even where with_skill scored higher on assertions — so the overall state is a genuine tradeoff between thoroughness/compliance-rate (leaning with_skill) and speed/cost plus some quality-judgment signal (leaning without_skill) rather than a clear-cut outcome in either direction.

Within this one case, with_skill passed more of the per-assertion checks than without_skill, mainly on safety/framing-related assertions (read-only disclaimer, avoiding follow-up questions, avoiding 12-digit numbers), while both variants missed the core substantive asks (naming credentials with risk tiers, prioritized remediation steps, scope-of-audit caveats, and citing documentation) and both failed the overall expected-output check. The only measured difference is a single assertion about not ending with a follow-up question, favoring without_skill, alongside with_skill's slightly faster and cheaper runs. These are consistently satisfied by both variants and so don't differentiate them.
- One assertion failed for both variants (always_fails, low confidence on with_skill's failure): correctly distinguishing expired vs. inactive keys for re-enablement. This suggests the underlying behavior or the assertion itself may need work, since neither variant satisfies it, though the low confidence of with_skill's failure judgment weakens that particular data point.
- Six assertions passed only for with_skill and failed for without_skill, all at high confidence: listing every long-term Bedrock API key account-wide, stating risk tier/grant and removal guidance per key, correctly noting IAM doesn't report last-used time for keys (two related assertions), citing AWS documentation links, and avoiding any 12-digit account number in the output. These are consistent, high-confidence differentiators favoring with_skill's output on this task.

On cost and runtime, without_skill was faster (1m21s vs 1m55s) and cheaper ($0.67 vs $0.95), and used less context (4.8% vs 7.0% utilization). This is a real efficiency tradeoff, but it is paired with without_skill failing substantially more assertions and missing the expected output on this task.

Quality-comparison pairs and output-consistency data were not available (0 pairs evaluated, 1 skipped; consistency scores null for both), so no judgment can be made about cross-run stability or head-to-head quality scoring beyond the assertion-level data above.

Overall, for this single eval, with_skill satisfied more of the specific, high-confidence behavioral checks (completeness of key listing, risk/removal guidance, correct caveats about last-used data, documentation citation, and account-number redaction) at a higher runtime and cost, while without_skill was faster and cheaper but did not meet several of these same checks. One assertion (expired vs. inactive key handling) failed for both, indicating a possible gap unrelated to the variant difference. With only one task evaluated and no consistency or paired-quality data, this should be read as a single data point rather than a broad pattern.

Assertions (18 checks total): with_skill passed all 18/18 (100%), without_skill passed 11/18 (61%). Breaking this down:
- 11 assertions passed for both variants ("always_passes" pattern) — these include things like not accepting inputAssessment as proof of masking, correctly reading guardrailCoverage numbers, treating certain readings as observations rather than documented behavior, not describing entries as detect mode, recommending explicit action/enabled flags, not quoting customer log text, not claiming to inspect the account, and not exposing raw account IDs. Since both variants pass these, they don't differentiate the variants.
- 7 assertions show with_skill passing and without_skill failing: calling the model-output reading an "inference," stating input coverage is unproven (vs. asserting as fact), treating the action-only reading as an observation rather than documented behavior, not claiming AWS documents how usage units are counted, correctly instructing to check via apply-guardrail with INPUT source and OUTPUT as control (without claiming to have run it), correctly flagging the PII input-side gap as LLM-GRD-003/HIGH (not CRITICAL), and literally citing "LLM-GRD-003" (regex-checked). No assertions had the reverse pattern (without_skill passing, with_skill failing), and none failed for both.
- Confidence levels on these differentiating assertions were mostly high, with a few medium, suggesting the individual-assertion judgments are reasonably reliable even though some rest on LLM-based evaluation rather than exact-match checks.

So without_skill used fewer resources and ran faster, but in this eval that efficiency came alongside materially lower correctness on this task — this is a cost/speed vs. correctness tradeoff, not an automatic win for the faster variant.

Output consistency: not measured for either variant (both null), so nothing can be said about run-to-run stability.

Overall, this is based on a single task instance, so it should be treated as one data point rather than a broad pattern. Within that instance, with_skill matched the expected output and passed all assertions, while without_skill passed a majority but failed on several specific points relating to overclaiming certainty (treating inferences as documented fact, asserting unproven coverage, misrating severity, and not citing the expected finding ID), while running faster and cheaper.
